questions.q: Write the nuclear equation for the α-decay of \(^{226}_{88}\text{Ra}\). Identify the daughter nucleus.
questions.a: \(^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow ^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}\). The daughter is radon-222 (\(^{222}_{86}\text{Rn}\)). A wrong answer (e.g., wrong Z or A) reveals the student does not conserve nucleon number and proton number separately in nuclear reactions.

questions.q: In β⁻ decay, a neutron transforms into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino. Explain why the atomic number Z increases by 1 while the mass number A remains unchanged.
questions.a: The neutron (n) → proton (p) + electron (e⁻) + antineutrino (\(\bar{\nu}_e\)). The proton stays in the nucleus, increasing Z by 1; the electron is emitted as the β⁻ particle. Total nucleons (A) unchanged because a nucleon merely changes type. A wrong answer (e.g., "A decreases") shows confusion between losing a nucleon and converting one.

questions.q: Given atomic masses: \(m(^{14}_{6}\text{C}) = 14.003242\,\text{u}\), \(m(^{14}_{7}\text{N}) = 14.003074\,\text{u}\). Calculate the Q-value (in MeV) for the β⁻ decay of carbon-14. Use 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c².
questions.a:
Step 1: Write decay: \(^{14}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow ^{14}_{7}\text{N} + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e\).  
Step 2: Q = [m(¹⁴C) - m(¹⁴N)]c². (Atomic masses include electrons; the emitted electron is accounted for because the daughter atom has one extra electron.)  
Step 3: Δm = 14.003242 u - 14.003074 u = 0.000168 u.  
Step 4: Q = 0.000168 u × 931.5 MeV/u = 0.1565 MeV ≈ 156.5 keV.  
A wrong sign or using nuclear masses without electron correction reveals misunderstanding of atomic vs nuclear mass in Q-value calculations.

questions.q: Compare the penetration ability of α, β, and γ radiation through paper, aluminum foil (3 mm), and lead (1 cm). Which radiation is stopped by each? Explain the physical reason for the order.
questions.a: Paper stops α (high charge +2e, large mass → strong ionization, short range). Aluminum foil (3 mm) stops β (charge -e, small mass → moderate ionization). Lead (1 cm) significantly attenuates γ (no charge, no mass → weak interaction, high penetration). A wrong ordering indicates confusion between ionizing power and penetration depth.

questions.q: A student writes the β⁺ decay of \(^{22}_{11}\text{Na}\) as: \(^{22}_{11}\text{Na} \rightarrow ^{22}_{10}\text{Ne} + e^+\). Is this equation complete? If not, what is missing and why must it be included for conservation laws?
questions.a:
Incomplete. Missing: electron neutrino (\(
u_e\)). The correct equation: \(^{22}_{11}	ext{Na} ightarrow ^{22}_{10}	ext{Ne} + e^+ + 
u_e\). The neutrino carries away missing energy, momentum, and lepton number (Lₑ: 0 → +1 for e⁺ and -1 for \(
u_e\)? Actually lepton number: e⁺ has Lₑ = -1, \(
u_e\) has Lₑ = +1, total 0). Without it, energy/momentum and lepton number conservation would be violated. A student omitting the neutrino thinks only charge and nucleon number matter.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a Geiger-Müller counter, a set of absorbers (paper, aluminum, lead), and a mixed α-β-γ source to identify which radiation type is which. Describe the procedure and expected count-rate pattern.
questions.a: Procedure: Place source near GM tube, record background-subtracted count rate R₀. Insert paper → count rate drops sharply (α stopped). Remove paper, insert 3 mm Al → further drop (β stopped). Remove Al, insert 1 cm Pb → count rate reduces but not to zero (γ attenuated). The remaining counts are γ. A poor answer lacks systematic absorber sequencing or fails to link count-rate changes to specific radiation properties.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The SI unit of activity (decays per second) is the ______ (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay/s.
Fill in the blank: Observe a smoke detector at home — it contains a tiny americium-241 source that emits alpha ______ to ionize air.
What is Radioactivity? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: The SI unit of activity (decays per second) is the becquerel (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay/s.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Radioactivity?
questions.a: Students often think γ-decay changes the element (Z or A) because they confuse it with α/β decay.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write balanced nuclear equations for α, β⁻, β⁺, and γ decays, identify the daughter nucleus (Z, A) from the parent, and explain how each decay changes the neutron-to-proton ratio to move toward the valley of stability.
